query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small trace amount (on the order of 0.5–1 atomic percent) of yttrium (Y) to the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will lead to enhanced grain-boundary stabilization and formation of protective yttrium-rich oxide films during service. This, in turn, will improve resistance to room-temperature creep, reduce microstructural coarsening under cyclic thermal fluctuations, and mitigate corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with a fine uniform lamellar fcc/B2 (or fcc/L12) structure exhibiting good strength and ductility but limited high-temperature creep and corrosion performance.
generation.intervention: Introduce 0.5–1 at.% Y into the alloy during melting and casting to enable trace rare-earth segregation to grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Standard industrial casting and thermomechanical processing conditions followed by exposure to cyclic thermal fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading at room temperature, and corrosive environments (e.g., salt-spray or molten salt tests) relevant to aerospace applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain-boundary segregation of yttrium leads to the formation of stable, thin yttrium oxide films and possibly nanoscale Y-rich intermetallic particles at or near boundaries, which pin grain boundaries and retard creep and corrosion mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: The yttrium addition preferentially segregates to grain boundaries, reducing grain-boundary energy and mobility. During cyclic thermal exposure and mechanical loading, these Y-rich sites form protective oxide layers that impede grain-boundary sliding (reducing creep) and block corrosive attack. This mechanism stabilizes the microstructure under extreme service conditions without significantly altering the intrinsic strength–ductility synergy of the lamellar eutectic structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the Y-doped variant is expected to show (i) at least a 20–30% reduction in room-temperature creep rate under long-term loading, (ii) improved stability of the fine lamellar microstructure under cyclic temperature variations (reduced grain coarsening by approximately 15–25%), and (iii) enhanced corrosion resistance as measured by a reduction in oxide spallation area and lower corrosion current densities in accelerated corrosion tests.
generation.baseline: The current as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with a uniform fine lamellar structure, which has good strength and ductility but exhibits limitations in long-term creep, thermal stability under cyclic loading, and corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable for components that operate within the temperature range up to approximately 700°C (and with cyclic fluctuations around room temperature to moderate high temperatures) and in corrosive environments relevant to aerospace fasteners. Extreme environments beyond these limits may require further modifications.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal yttrium concentration is not predetermined and excessive Y could lead to the formation of undesirable brittle phases or segregation that impairs ductility. Moreover, the interplay between Y-induced grain-boundary stabilization and possible effects on phase equilibrium within the eutectic structure remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and another with 0.5–1 at.% Y addition using identical casting and processing routes. Subject both sets to accelerated testing including (i) room temperature creep tests under constant load over extended periods, (ii) cyclic thermal loading tests simulating aerospace service conditions, and (iii) corrosion evaluations using salt spray or molten salt assays.
measurements: Creep rate and time-to-failure under constant stress at room temperature
Grain coarsening and microstructural stability (via SEM/TEM) before and after cyclic thermal tests
Corrosion current densities, oxide scale adherence, and spallation area measurements during corrosion testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., >20% reduction in creep rate, measurable enhancement in microstructural stability, and appreciably lower corrosion metrics) compared to the baseline alloy, or if the ductility and strength deteriorate substantially due to embrittlement or undesirable phase formation, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5). papers.title: Enhanced strength-ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae.
papers.approach: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing to inherit the as‐cast lamellar geometry and induce phase decomposition for a duplex ultrafine-grained structure
papers.findings: The processed alloy achieved a superior combination of high strength and ductility compared to traditional routes; in particular, the imposed hierarchical structure led to concurrent improvements by invoking two-hierarchical constraint effects and microcrack-arresting mechanisms.
papers.mechanism: The composite lamellar architecture provides simultaneous strengthening (by refined grain sizes and hard phase contributions) and ductility (by retaining soft phase regions), where inherited lamellae induce a two-hierarchical constraint and arrest microcrack propagation.

papers.title: A promising new class of high-temperature alloys: eutectic high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Eutectic alloy design via a pseudo-binary multi‐component system to achieve a fine lamellar fcc/B2 (or fcc/L12) microstructure with excellent castability
papers.findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and fracture strength at room temperature that could be maintained up to 700°C, offering a pathway for industrial-scale production.
papers.mechanism: The alternating soft (fcc) and hard (B2) phases in the lamellar structure enable load partitioning and simultaneous high deformation resistance and ductility.

papers.title: Small-scale mechanical behavior of a eutectic high entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Evaluation of phase-specific mechanical properties using nano-indentation and micro-pillar compression tests
papers.findings: The B2 phase demonstrated higher hardness and yield strength compared to the L12 phase. Mixed pillars exhibited dual yielding and well-preserved interfaces, indicating that the dual-phase microstructure controls overall deformation.
papers.mechanism: Load partitioning between phases, enhanced by the integrity of the phase boundaries, leads to an overall mechanical response that is closer to that of the stronger B2 phase.

papers.title: Influence of ordered L1₂ precipitation on strain-rate dependent mechanical behavior in a eutectic high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloy (Al₀.₇CoCrFeNi) with lamellar fcc + B2 structure
papers.approach: Introducing low-temperature annealing to precipitate ordered L1₂ (or L12) intermetallic phases within the ductile fcc matrix
papers.findings: The formation of coherent nano-scale L1₂ precipitates significantly increased the yield strength under both quasi-static and dynamic loading, while largely preserving strain rate sensitivity and ductility.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanisms reinforces the fcc phase, enhancing strength without a major detriment to plasticity.

papers.title: Simultaneous Strength-Ductility Enhancement of a Nano-Lamellar AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ Eutectic High Entropy Alloy by Cryo-Rolling and Annealing.
papers.approach: Utilizing a combination of cryo-rolling followed by annealing to produce a hierarchical microstructure with both fine lamellar and non-lamellar regions
papers.findings: The processed alloy exhibited significantly enhanced strength (e.g., yield strength around 1437 MPa) and ductility (elongation ~14%) compared to the as-cast state through strain-partitioning and controlled recrystallization effects.
papers.mechanism: Cryo-deformation stores high strain energy promoting heterogeneous transformation during subsequent annealing, leading to regions with ultrafine grains and retained interfaces that contribute to simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility.

papers.title: Thermal Stability and Hot Corrosion Performance of the AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ High-Entropy Alloy Coating by Laser Cladding.
papers.approach: Laser cladding to produce coatings, with subsequent heat treatment and evaluation under high-temperature (900°C) hot corrosion conditions (molten salt exposure)
papers.findings: Coatings retained dual-phase microstructures after heat treatment, with the precipitation of an Al-rich L1₂ phase; minor compositional modification (Y and Hf co-doping) improved thermal stability and reduced corrosion oxide spallation.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced thermal stability derives from controlled grain growth and the formation of protective precipitates, while improved corrosion resistance is linked to the reduction in spallation of the oxide scale.

papers.title: From Small Data Modeling to Large Language Model Screening: A Dual-Strategy Framework for Materials Intelligent Design.
papers.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (including comparisons with AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ and newly designed variants)
papers.approach: Combining adversarial domain adaptation with automated screening to identify new alloy compositions based on data-driven insights
papers.findings: A novel eutectic HEA with enhanced plasticity and comparable strength to AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ was identified, demonstrating a pathway to mitigate processing limitations and performance constraints.
papers.mechanism: Data-guided design integrates predictive modeling with extended compositional variations to identify combinations that may overcome the conventional strength–ductility tradeoff by subtle compositional adjustments.

established: The eutectic design strategy in AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ alloys yields a fine lamellar microstructure combining soft (fcc) and hard (B2 or L1₂) phases, resulting in improved strength–ductility balance.
Thermo-mechanical processing (e.g., cryo-rolling, cold rolling, and annealing) can induce hierarchical and heterogeneous microstructures that further enhance performance.
Ordered precipitate formation (such as L1₂) within the fcc phase effectively increases yield strength without a major loss in ductility.
EHEAs exhibit promising high-temperature mechanical properties and castability, with performance maintained up to 700°C.

approaches_tried.approach: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing to inherit and refine lamellar microstructures
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced strength–ductility synergy through duplex ultrafine-grained structures and improved load partitioning

approaches_tried.approach: Introducing ordered precipitates (L1₂) via low-temperature annealing
approaches_tried.outcome: Increased yield strength with maintained ductility under various strain rates

approaches_tried.approach: Laser cladding with minor elemental modifications (Y and Hf co-doping)
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved thermal stability and enhanced hot corrosion resistance

approaches_tried.approach: Data-driven alloy screening and design to identify alternative eutectic compositions
approaches_tried.outcome: Identification of alloys with enhanced plasticity and comparable strength to the starting material

mechanisms: Composite lamellar architecture providing hierarchical constraint and load partitioning
Precipitation strengthening via coherent intermetallic phases (L1₂) and dislocation-obstacle interactions
Strain-induced refinement and heterogeneous recrystallization enhancing both strength and ductility
Improved oxide scale adhesion and grain boundary stabilization for thermal and corrosion resistance
disagreements: The optimal balance between strengthening via precipitate formation and retaining ductility remains under debate, especially when further modifications are needed for resistance to creep and corrosion.

There is uncertainty regarding the long-term stability of the microstructural phases under cyclic temperature fluctuations and continuous load, with some studies suggesting potential phase instability.
open_questions: How can the current eutectic microstructure be further engineered to mitigate creep under long-term mechanical loading?
What specific compositional or processing intervention would better improve corrosion resistance without compromising the strength–ductility balance?
How will the modified alloy microstructure perform under cyclic thermal fluctuations typical in aerospace applications?
What are the effects of potential interstitial additions or grain boundary doping on the stability of the lamellar structure during extended service?
opportunities: Investigating a single compositional intervention, such as introducing trace alloying elements (e.g., Y, Hf, or interstitial atoms) to promote grain boundary stabilization, could enhance both high-temperature creep resistance and corrosion stability.

Combining advanced thermo-mechanical processing (e.g., cryo-rolling followed by controlled annealing) with targeted elemental doping may yield a microstructure that further resists phase coarsening under cyclic loads and thermal fluctuations.

Exploring in situ precipitation and dynamic phase transformation mechanisms during service conditions can provide design guidelines for simultaneously enhancing long-term mechanical reliability and corrosion resistance.

Utilization of data-driven screening tools to predict subtle compositional modifications that specifically benefit properties under extreme service conditions offers a promising avenue for future experimental validation.

directions.direction: Trace rare‐earth microalloying (e.g., adding Y) to promote grain-boundary segregation and stabilization.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets long-term heat and creep stability as well as corrosion resistance by forming stable, protective oxide layers at grain boundaries. Prior studies (e.g., PMC10488378) show that Y (often co‐doped with Hf) can improve thermal stability and reduce oxide spallation in related HEA coatings. The underlying physics of reactive element segregation to grain boundaries is well established; while the optimal level must be tuned, the intervention is feasible and impactful.

directions.direction: Interstitial doping with light elements (such as C or B) to strengthen grain boundaries.
directions.assessment: Interstitial additions could increase creep resistance and improve corrosion performance by reducing grain-boundary sliding. However, this path risks carbide or boride formation that might embrittle the material, making the mechanism less direct with respect to the strength–ductility balance.

directions.direction: Modified thermo-mechanical processing to induce optimized fine-scale precipitation and an evolved dual-phase lamellar interface.
directions.assessment: Advanced processing (e.g., a combination of cryo-rolling and controlled low-temperature annealing) can refine microstructures and precipitate ordered phases like L1₂, which have been shown to improve yield strength (see PMC6478865). Nonetheless, this route may not directly address long-term thermal stability and creep resistance under cyclic service conditions.

directions.direction: Surface treatments or protective coatings tailored to the alloy to mitigate corrosion and creep.
directions.assessment: Applying a corrosion-resistant coating could improve performance under harsh portions of the service environment. However, it does not modify the bulk microstructure and may not fully address creep under mechanical loading, making it a less integrated solution.

directions.direction: Data-driven compositional tuning using machine learning to identify subtle composition shifts for balancing phase stability and interface strength.
directions.assessment: Modeling-based approaches offer the chance to screen broader compositional spaces to optimize phase stability. Yet, while promising, they require confirmatory synthesis and may not be easily linked to direct improvements in creep and corrosion without clear intervention on grain boundaries.

choice.direction: Trace rare‐earth microalloying (Y additions) to improve grain-boundary stability
choice.why: This approach directly addresses the combined challenges of long-term creep, thermal cycling, and corrosion resistance by stabilizing the grain boundaries. Its feasibility is supported by coating studies (as in PMC10488378) and the well-known benefits of reactive element additions in high-temperature applications, while having limited impact on the inherent strength–ductility balance of the eutectic microstructure.
